extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning discrete mathematics / relations
extracted.subtask_description: Textbook chapter-level guidance defining relations on sets, the properties reflexive/symmetric/transitive, equivalence relations and classes, partitions, and the integers modulo n, with examples and methods of proof. Intended for students learning how to recognise, represent, and prove properties of relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation as subset of A×A
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R on a set A is a subset R ⊆ A × A; the expression xRy means (x,y) ∈ R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relations can be listed as sets of ordered pairs, described in set-builder notation, or drawn as diagrams. Any subset of A×A is a relation, whether or not it 'means' anything familiar. Example: R = > on Z can be written R = {(x,y) ∈ Z×Z : x - y ∈ N}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation: diagrams (arrow notation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Depict (x,y) ∈ R by an arrow pointing from x to y; the picture then represents which ordered pairs are in R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagrams often convey relations more intuitively than listing pairs, and can help spot properties. Limitations: diagrams are impractical or impossible for large/infinite sets; use set-builder notation for infinite relations. Example: drawing nodes labelled by elements of B and arrows for U in Example 11.4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation: set-builder notation for infinite relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use set-builder notation to describe relations on infinite sets (e.g., R = {(x,y) ∈ Z×Z : x - y ∈ N}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set-builder notation succinctly expresses infinite relations that cannot be drawn. Example: the '>' relation on Z is given as R = {(x,y) ∈ Z×Z : x - y ∈ N}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflexive (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relation R on A is reflexive if xRx for every x ∈ A. Formally: R is reflexive if ∀x ∈ A, xRx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To check reflexivity verify every element has a loop in the diagram. Examples: =, | (divides), and ≤ are reflexive on appropriate sets. Counterexamples: >, <, ≠ are not reflexive. In diagrams a loop at each point indicates reflexivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetric (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relation R on A is symmetric if xRy implies yRx for all x,y ∈ A. Formally: ∀x,y ∈ A, (xRy) ⇒ (yRx).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In diagrams, symmetry means whenever there is an arrow x→y there is an arrow y→x. Examples: = and 'has same parity as' are symmetric. Non-example: < is not symmetric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitive (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relation R on A is transitive if whenever xRy and yRz then xRz. Formally: ∀x,y,z ∈ A, [(xRy ∧ yRz) ⇒ xRz].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In diagrams, transitivity requires that arrows x→y and y→z imply an arrow x→z (possibly a loop if x = z). Examples: <, >, = are transitive. To verify, check all triples (or use structure/meaning of the relation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spotting properties from diagrams (visual tests)
rubrics_metrics.description: How to recognize reflexive, symmetric, and transitive properties from a relation diagram: loops at all points for reflexive; for every arrow x→y there is y→x for symmetric; arrows x→y and y→z imply x→z for transitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the three visual checks summarized in the boxes: (1) reflexive ↔ loop at each point; (2) symmetric ↔ every arrow has a reverse; (3) transitive ↔ composable arrows yield the composed arrow. Note limitations for large/infinite relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operations on relations produce relations (intersection/union/etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set-operations on relations (e.g., R ∩ S, R ∪ S) yield relations on the same set A; logical combinations correspond to set operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: x ∈ (R ∩ S) means x satisfies both R and S simultaneously; Example 11.3: R∩S = {(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(3,1),(4,4),(4,2)} and x(R∩S)y means 'x>y and x,y have same parity.' Use these operations to build complex relations from simpler ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relation (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R on A is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalence relations commonly express a notion of 'sameness' (equality or a weaker equivalence like same parity). Examples and diagrams (Figure 11.2) illustrate several different equivalence relations on the same set with different equivalence-class partitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence class [a] (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an equivalence relation R on A and a ∈ A, the equivalence class containing a is [a] = { x ∈ A : xRa }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalence classes collect all elements equivalent to a. Examples: for = (mod n), [0] = {...,-3,0,3,6,...}. Note [2] = [4] in the parity example. Important property: [a] = [b] iff aRb (Theorem 11.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence classes partition A (theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of equivalence classes {[a] : a ∈ A} of an equivalence relation R forms a partition of A: the union equals A and distinct classes are disjoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses reflexive/symmetric/transitive properties. Conversely, any partition of A defines an equivalence relation by declaring xRy iff x and y lie in the same part. Examples: partitions induced by = (mod n) give the classes [0],[1],...,[n-1].

rubrics_metrics.name: Integers modulo n as equivalence classes and arithmetic
rubrics_metrics.description: For fixed n ∈ N, congruence mod n is an equivalence relation on Z with classes [0],[1],...,[n-1]; the set Zn = {[0],...,[n-1]} can be given addition and multiplication by [a]+[b]=[a+b] and [a]·[b]=[ab].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use representatives but remember equal classes must be identified (e.g., [5]=[0] in Z5). Tables illustrate arithmetic on Zn. Examples and explicit class descriptions for n=3 and n=5 are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof techniques for properties of relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use direct proofs and the defining properties (e.g., divisibility) to prove reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity. For instance, prove congruence mod n is reflexive, symmetric and transitive by using divisibility and manipulation of equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show step-by-step direct proofs: (1) reflexive: show n|(x-x); (2) symmetric: from n|(x-y) deduce n|(y-x) by multiplying by -1; (3) transitive: add equations n|(x-y) and n|(y-z) to get n|(x-z). Follow the quantifier structure in the formal definitions when writing proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning is helpful but not required
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation need not have an intuitive 'meaning'; any subset of A×A is a relation even if no familiar interpretation exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cautions that some relations are random subsets with no obvious meaning (Example 11.4). However, when a meaning exists it often simplifies understanding and proofs (see Example 11.7 where xRy means 'both consonants').
